title: "Lost John," the miner under the boulder in Mammoth Cave
summary: In 1935, guides deep in Mammoth Cave found the body of an adult man pinned under a huge boulder. He was a pre-Columbian miner who had been digging out cave minerals and…
bodyMarkdown:
Deep inside what is now [Mammoth Cave National Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mammoth_Cave_National_Park), Early Woodland people mined the dry upper passages for more than a thousand years. From about 1000 to 200 BCE they entered the Mammoth Cave system with river-cane torches, mussel-shell scrapers, limestone hammerstones, and woven fiber sandals. Archaeologists have traced their work for many miles underground. They scraped gypsum, mirabilite, and related sulfate minerals from the walls. What they did with those minerals is not settled. [Park and survey accounts](https://www.nps.gov/maca/learn/historyculture/native-americans.htm) note that gypsum may have served as paint, that mirabilite can act as a laxative and has a salty taste that could season or preserve food, and that the minerals may also have been traded or used in ritual. There is no direct proof of any single use.

These were not occasional visitors. Native explorers discovered more than nineteen miles of passageways inside the park. They also left cane baskets, wooden climbing poles, gourd and squash containers, and pictographs drawn with the charred tips of their torches—cross-hatched, rectilinear, and spiral designs on the stone. Men seem to have done most of the mining. Some archaeologists think the caves may also have held coming-of-age ceremonies, though that too is an inference, not a proven fact.

Mining and deep exploration tapered off after about 200 BCE. The [Kentucky Archaeological Survey](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Mammoth-Cave.aspx) suggests changing beliefs and traditions as a likely reason. The dry air of the cave preserved what the miners left behind—torch stubs, scrapers, sandals, and, in a few places, human remains.

In 1935, cave guides Grover Campbell and Lyman Cutliff, working with a Civilian Conservation Corps trail crew, found the body of an adult man pinned under a huge boulder on a high ledge. He had been mining. When he disturbed the rubble that held the rock, it shifted and settled onto him. The dry cave air naturally mummified him. Artifacts with the remains pointed to an age of more than 2,000 years, placing him in the same Early Woodland mining culture that worked the cave for gypsum and other minerals.

The find was one of the most important archaeological moments in the park’s history. The remains were studied, then displayed to visitors along a tour route for decades. Guides called him “Lost John.” He stayed on view into the 1970s. Growing concern over the public display of Native American remains, and later federal and state law, ended that practice. The park reburied him in a secret location inside the cave, away from tour traffic, after consulting with affiliated tribes.

The exact ledge and passage are not published. Mammoth Cave National Park is a public place, and the Historic Entrance that visitors use is not the find site. Digging or collecting without permission is illegal. The story of this miner belongs with the larger Woodland use of the cave system, not with a named portrait of one man. Other Early Woodland cave work in the same country is told in the [Salts Cave](/stories/salts-cave-15ht4/) story.

## Kentucky today

Mammoth Cave National Park interprets prehistoric mining on its tours and in its museum without pointing visitors to any burial. The Early Woodland gypsum mines remain one of the clearest records of how deeply Kentucky’s first farmers explored underground—and what those journeys could cost.
